prompt: For a monochrome bitmap image, each pixel requires:
explanation: Monochrome means two states, black or white, and one bit gives exactly two states. The general rule is that k bits per pixel give 2 to the power k colours.

why.a: Wrong. 2 bits give 4 levels, which is a four-shade image rather than a monochrome one.
why.b: Wrong. 8 bits give 256 levels, the usual greyscale depth.
why.c: Correct. One bit, two states, so image size in bits equals the number of pixels.
why.d: Wrong. 4 bits give 16 levels, the old 16-colour standard.

prompt: Photographs are generally better represented using:
explanation: A photograph is continuous tone with no clean edges to describe as shapes, so it is stored as a grid of pixel values. Pair this with the logo question, where the answer was vector.

why.a: Wrong. Vectors describe shapes with equations, which suits logos and diagrams, not the texture of a real scene.
why.c: Wrong. Excess-3 encodes single decimal digits.
why.d: Correct. A pixel grid captures continuous tone, which is what a photograph is.

prompt: A processor fetches an instruction while simultaneously reading data from memory. Which architecture makes this possible?
explanation: Harvard keeps instructions and data in separate memories with separate buses, so both can be read in the same cycle.

why.a: Wrong. Stack architecture describes how operands are addressed, not how memory is wired.
why.b: Wrong. CISC is an instruction set philosophy, unrelated to the number of memory paths.
why.c: Wrong, and this is the contrast being tested. Von Neumann shares ONE memory and one bus for both, which forces the two accesses to take turns. That queue is the Von Neumann bottleneck.
why.d: Correct. Separate paths mean genuinely simultaneous access.

prompt: An embedded system uses separate memory modules for instructions and data to improve throughput. Which architectural design is being used?
explanation: The phrase SEPARATE MEMORY for instructions and data is the definition of Harvard. It is common in embedded and signal processing designs for exactly the throughput reason given.

why.a: Wrong. Von Neumann is the SINGLE shared memory design, the opposite of what the stem describes.
why.b: Wrong. Stack architecture is about operand addressing, not memory separation.
why.c: Wrong. Pipelining overlaps the stages of instruction processing. It is a technique, not a memory arrangement, though Harvard helps it along.
why.d: Correct. Separate instruction and data memories.

prompt: Which characteristic is a major advantage of the Harvard Architecture?

options.text: Single memory space for all data
Simultaneous access to instructions and data

explanation: Two memories with two buses means an instruction fetch and a data read can happen at once, which raises throughput and removes the Von Neumann bottleneck.

why.a: Wrong, and it describes VON NEUMANN. Harvard deliberately splits the memory space in two.
why.b: Wrong, and backwards. Two memory systems and two bus sets are MORE hardware, which is the price Harvard pays.
why.c: Correct. Both accesses in the same cycle.
why.d: Wrong. Splitting memory does not reduce how much is needed, and fixed separate pools can waste space when one fills before the other.
